title: The open-source data stack
summary: A layer-by-layer map of the open-source data stack, and how to choose between self-hosting and buying.

blocks.text: Almost every managed data product has an open-source counterpart, and many managed products are built on open-source cores (Kafka, Spark, Iceberg, Airflow, Trino). Knowing the open components by layer helps you read vendor offerings, design a portable platform, and decide where self-hosting is worth it.

blocks.text: Kafka-API compatibility is a de facto standard. Choosing tools that speak it keeps you free to switch brokers or move to a managed service later.

The table format is the most strategic choice because it outlives engines. Iceberg has the broadest multi-engine support and an open REST catalog protocol; Delta Lake is deeply integrated with Spark and Databricks; Hudi is strong for record-level upserts and incremental pulls. Chapters 21 to 25 cover Iceberg in depth.

items: **Hive Metastore**: the legacy catalog; widely supported but has no multi-table transactions and weak support for modern table-format commits.
**Project Nessie**: a catalog with Git-like branches, tags and multi-table commits over Iceberg.
**Apache Polaris**: an implementation of the Iceberg REST catalog specification with role-based access control; incubating at Apache, so check the current documentation for status and features.
Other REST-compatible catalogs exist (for example Unity Catalog OSS, Lakekeeper, Gravitino). The REST spec is what lets different engines share one catalog (chapter 24).

head: Engine
Sweet spot
Not ideal for
rows: Large batch ETL, ML pipelines, writes to table formats
Interactive SQL federated across many sources and Iceberg
Very long ETL jobs (fault tolerance is opt-in)
In-process analytics on one machine; GB to low TB; local dev and CI
Real-time OLAP serving with very fast aggregations (chapter 46)
Frequent row updates, complex multi-table joins at scale

blocks.text: A common combination: Spark or Flink write Iceberg, Trino and DuckDB read it interactively, and ClickHouse serves a few latency-critical dashboards from a curated copy.

items: **Airflow / Dagster** for orchestration (chapter 30).
**dbt Core / SQLMesh** for SQL transformation (chapter 31). dbt Core is open source; some dbt features such as the hosted semantic layer API are part of the commercial platform.
**Great Expectations** (Python expectation suites) and **Soda Core** (YAML-based checks in SodaCL) for data quality (chapter 33).
**OpenLineage** is a standard event spec for lineage emitted by Airflow, Spark, dbt and Flink integrations; **Marquez** is its reference metadata server and UI.
**Apache Superset** for dashboards and SQL exploration on top of Trino, ClickHouse and others.

blocks.text: 32.6 How to choose: build vs buy
Open source is free to download, not free to run. The real decision is about where your team's engineering hours create the most value.

head: Factor
Favours self-hosted OSS
Favours managed / commercial
rows: Very large, steady workloads where infrastructure margin matters
Platform team with Kubernetes, JVM and on-call experience
Small data team focused on modelling
Data residency, air-gapped or custom requirements
Standard compliance covered by vendor certifications
Can afford months of platform build
Open formats are critical to strategy
Accepts vendor APIs, mitigated by open formats underneath

items: **Infrastructure**: compute, storage, network egress, monitoring.
**People**: a self-hosted Kafka, Trino or Airflow deployment easily needs a fraction of an engineer each for upgrades, tuning and on-call. Several components add up to a team.
**Risk**: security patches, CVE response, upgrade breakage, knowledge concentrated in few engineers.
**Opportunity cost**: hours spent operating clusters are not spent on data products.

blocks.text: A frequent failure: assembling ten self-hosted components for a data team of four. Each is reasonable alone; together they consume the team. Start with the fewest moving parts and add components when a real need appears.

Licences change. Several data projects have moved between permissive and source-available licences. Check the current licence of each component, and its governance (foundation-hosted or single-vendor), before betting on it.

blocks.title: A mid-size company picks a hybrid
blocks.text: A logistics company with a six-person data platform team wanted open formats but limited operations. They chose:
items: Managed Kafka with Debezium in Kafka Connect for CDC; Iceberg on object storage with a managed REST catalog.
Self-hosted Trino for interactive queries, because query volume was high and steady.
Dagster for orchestration and dbt Core for transformations, run in CI with DuckDB for fast tests.
Superset for internal dashboards; OpenLineage events from dbt and Spark jobs sent to a lineage backend.

blocks.title: Design a stack for two scenarios
blocks.text: Scenario A: a 3-person analytics team at a startup with 200 GB of data from Postgres and five SaaS tools. Scenario B: a bank's platform team of 20 with 2 PB, strict data residency and several query engines. For each, choose components per layer, mark what is self-hosted versus managed, and estimate where operational effort will concentrate.
hints: Which layers can you skip entirely in scenario A?
Which choice in scenario B is hardest to reverse later?

items: Map the stack by layer: ingestion, streaming, table format, catalog, engines, orchestration, transformation, quality, lineage, BI.
The table format and catalog protocol are the most strategic, longest-lived choices.
Engines are specialised: Spark for batch ETL, Trino for interactive federation, DuckDB for single-node, ClickHouse for real-time OLAP.
OpenLineage standardises lineage events across tools.
Total cost of ownership is dominated by people and risk, not licences; start small and add components on real need.

blocks.q: Which open component is primarily a log-based CDC connector?
blocks.explain: Debezium reads database transaction logs and emits change events, usually through Kafka Connect. dlt is a Python loading library, Trino a query engine and Marquez a lineage server.

blocks.q: Why is the Iceberg REST catalog specification important for an open stack?
options: It lets different engines share one catalog through a standard protocol
blocks.explain: The REST spec decouples engines from catalog implementations, so Spark, Trino, Flink and warehouses can commit to and read the same tables. Compression and compaction are separate concerns.

blocks.q: A four-person team plans to self-host Kafka, Flink, Trino, Airflow, Nessie and Superset. What is the main concern?
options: Licence fees will be too high
Operational load will exceed the team's capacity
blocks.explain: Each component needs upgrades, tuning and on-call; together they can consume a small team. Licences are usually not the cost driver, and these tools integrate fine.

blocks.q: Which engine best fits fast tests of SQL models in CI on a laptop or runner?
blocks.explain: DuckDB is an in-process engine that starts instantly and handles moderate data on one machine. Hive Metastore is a catalog, Kafka Connect moves data, and Flink is a streaming engine.
